title: Web apps
description: The templates/web-app starter for streaming demo applications, the responsiveness rules it encodes, and the Source interface a device driver implements.

import Callout from '@ambiqai/helia-ui/astro/Callout';

Live WebUSB and Bluetooth demos, streaming dashboards and interactive tooling
are React and TypeScript applications built with Vite, not Starlight sites. They
consume `tokens.css`, `tailwind.css` and `react/*` so they look like the docs
that link to them, and they live in their own repositories.

`templates/web-app/` is the starter. It ships a working example: a top bar with
a connection Badge and a theme toggle, a control Card with a source Select, a
sample-rate Slider and a connect Button, a live Recharts trace fed at 50 to 250
Hz, and a status footer with toasts.

<Callout tone="note" title="The static-by-default rule does not apply here">
  Docs and marketing pages ship no JavaScript, and that is a hard rule. An app's
  bar is a different one: responsiveness under streaming. Trading a maintained
  component for a smaller bundle is the wrong trade in this lane.
</Callout>

## Which template

| The thing you are building                | Template                 |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Product documentation, reference, guides  | `templates/product-docs` |
| Live hardware, streaming data, dashboards | `templates/web-app`      |

Both are repo-only: neither is in the package's `files`, so neither is in the
published tarball. Copy them out of `AmbiqAI/helia-ui`.

## What the starter wires up

- **Vite, React 19 and strict TypeScript.** `npm run check` is `tsc --noEmit`
  and `npm run lint` is ESLint with the type-checked typescript-eslint rules
  plus `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`.
- **Tailwind v4 through `@tailwindcss/vite`**, with an entry that imports
  `tokens.css`, `semantic.css` and `tailwind.css` in the order the Starlight
  plugin uses, then Tailwind's Preflight, because an app has no docs shell to
  inherit a baseline from.
- **A theme toggle that owns `data-theme` on `<html>`.** Light, dark and system,
  persisted, applied before first paint by a small script in `index.html`.
- **A Pages deploy.** `vite.config.ts` reads `base` from `BASE_PATH`, and
  `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` passes the repository name so a project site's
  asset URLs carry the prefix.
- **A Playwright smoke test** that loads the built app, starts the simulated
  source, and asserts the chart receives data.

<Callout tone="caution" title="Name each React component in the scan list">
  Tailwind 4.3 applies its ignore rules to `@source` paths inside
  `node_modules`. Both `.../react` and `.../react/*.tsx` silently match nothing,
  so `text-foreground` and the rest are never emitted and the components render
  with the inherited text colour — which looks like a broken dark mode rather
  than a missing utility. One `@source` line per component file is the only form
  that gets through.
</Callout>

## Outside Starlight

A docs site gets a handful of variables from Starlight's own `props.css`. An app
has no Starlight, so the template's entry supplies them: the two system font
stacks and `--sl-color-text-invert`, restated at Starlight's values.

`data-theme` matters for the same reason. The tokens flip under
`:root[data-theme='light']` and the package's `dark:` variant keys on
`[data-theme='dark']`, so an app that leaves the attribute unset gets the dark
palette from the tokens while every `dark:` utility evaluates false. That is why
the template resolves `system` to a concrete value rather than clearing the
attribute.

## The responsiveness rules

A streaming app that ignores these feels broken on the machine the demo runs on,
which is not the machine it was written on.

1. **Generate and parse off the main thread.** The simulated signal runs in a
   Web Worker, and a real driver's packet decode belongs there too. A sample
   clock that shares the main thread drifts whenever React renders.
2. **Transfer, do not copy.** The worker posts `Float32Array` chunks with the
   buffer in the transfer list.
3. **Chunks, never samples.** A per-sample callback puts one JavaScript call on
   the main thread per sample, which is where the frame budget goes at the top
   of the rate range.
4. **Update state at display rate, not sample rate.** Chunks go straight into a
   fixed ring buffer, which is not React state and triggers nothing. One
   `requestAnimationFrame` publishes what is there. Everything that lands before
   the frame fires is already in the buffer, so coalescing loses no samples —
   only pictures nobody could have seen.
5. **Decimate before the chart, not in it.** The buffer returns a fixed number
   of points chosen against the trace's pixel width, so render cost stops being
   a function of the sample rate.
6. **No animation on a live series.** `isAnimationActive={false}`,
   `dot={false}`, a fixed axis domain, a linear line type. Recharts will
   otherwise restart an entry animation on every data change and never finish
   one.

The smoke test asserts the outcome rather than the mechanism: raising the source
from 100 Hz to 250 Hz must multiply the samples received without moving the
number of chart updates per second.

## The Source interface

One contract sits between the app shell and whatever produces samples. It is the
interface a real device driver implements, not a simplification of one.

```ts
export interface Source {
  readonly id: SourceId;
  readonly label: string;

  /** Synchronous feature detection. Never prompts, never touches the device. */
  support(): SourceSupport;

  /** Acquire the transport and start streaming. Rejects with a message fit for a toast. */
  connect(sampleRate: number): Promise<void>;

  /** Retune while connected. A control transfer or a GATT write on real hardware. */
  setSampleRate(sampleRate: number): void;

  /** Release the transport. Safe to call when already disconnected. */
  disconnect(): Promise<void>;

  /** Subscribe. Returns the unsubscribe function. */
  onChunk(listener: (chunk: StreamChunk) => void): () => void;
}
```

A chunk carries the samples and the rate they were produced at, and ownership
passes to the listener — a transferable arriving from a worker is already
detached on the producer's side.

The template ships three implementations. `SimulatedSource` is complete and
worker-backed. `WebUsbSource` and `BluetoothSource` are stubbed at exactly one
point each: everything above it is real, including the filtered chooser, the
interface claim or the GATT walk, and the teardown order. What is missing is the
decode, because the packet layout belongs to the board's firmware. Fill in the
read loop or the notification handler and nothing outside that file changes.

`support()` returning a reason rather than a bare boolean is deliberate. WebUSB
and Web Bluetooth are Chromium-only and secure-context-only, so "it did not
connect" and "this browser cannot connect" are different states and the
interface has to tell them apart. Both also gate the device chooser on a live
user activation, which an `await` consumes, so `connect()` must be called
directly from a click handler.

## Claims

Product status, support, maturity and performance statements are not authored in
a demo app any more than in a docs site. They come from the approved export of
the handbook's `portfolio.yaml`. The sample copy in the template is shape, not
copy.
